title: GMAT Focus Verbal Practice Test 25
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt: A rail freight operator introduced longer trains and reports that its cost per tonne carried has fallen. It concludes that longer trains are more economical.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. Longer trains require more powerful locomotives.
B. Drivers are paid per shift.
C. The operator runs fewer services than before.
D. Fuel prices fell during the period.
E. Several terminals cannot handle the longer trains, so freight for those destinations now travels by road at a cost the operator records separately.
questions.explanation: Traffic that no longer fits has been moved off the measure, so the cost per tonne describes a changed and easier set of journeys.

questions.prompt: A community pharmacy began offering flu vaccination and reports that its prescription dispensing volume rose in the same period. The owner concludes that the vaccination service brings in customers who then use the pharmacy for prescriptions.
questions.question: Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating the conclusion?
options: A. How much the vaccination service charges
B. Whether dispensing volumes rose by a similar amount at nearby pharmacies not offering vaccination
C. Whether the pharmacy advertised the service
D. How many staff the pharmacy employs
E. Whether the vaccine is supplied by the health service
questions.explanation: A seasonal or area-wide rise would produce the same figure; comparable pharmacies without the service settle which it is.

questions.prompt: A school canteen removed sugary drinks from sale and reports that pupils' consumption of sugary drinks at school fell to nothing. The head teacher concludes that pupils' sugar intake has fallen.
questions.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: A. ignores the revenue the canteen has lost
B. does not specify which drinks were removed
C. relies on data from a single term
D. assumes that consumption not occurring at school does not occur elsewhere
E. overlooks pupils who bring packed lunches
questions.explanation: The measure covers one location; pupils may buy the same drinks on the way to and from school, so total intake is unestablished.

questions.prompt: A car club reports that members drive fewer miles per year than the national average for car owners, and argues that joining a car club reduces driving.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the argument?
options: A. Car club vehicles are booked by the hour.
B. Some members also own a car.
C. People join car clubs when they already drive little, having decided that owning a car is not worth the cost.
D. Car club vehicles are newer than average.
E. The club operates in cities.
questions.explanation: The membership decision follows from low driving rather than causing it, so the comparison with owners is not informative about the club's effect.

questions.prompt: Every van operated by the Redhill hedge-trimming service that carries a chipper is fitted with a tracker. No vehicle fitted with a tracker has been involved in a reported speeding offence this year. Some of the service's vans have been involved in reported speeding offences this year.
questions.question: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true?
options: A. Some of the service's vans do not carry a chipper.
B. Trackers prevent speeding.
C. Most vans carry chippers.
D. Vans with chippers travel more slowly.
E. Drivers of untracked vans are less experienced.
questions.explanation: Vans with offences have no tracker, and carrying a chipper implies a tracker, so those vans carry no chipper. B asserts a causal claim the premises do not establish.

questions.prompt: A textile mill installed monitoring equipment on its looms and reports that unplanned stoppages fell by a third in the following year. Management concludes that the equipment predicts faults before they occur.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the conclusion?
options: A. The equipment was supplied by the loom manufacturer.
B. Staff received training on the new system.
C. The mill also replaced several older looms.
D. Stoppages are recorded automatically.
E. Maintenance records show that most of the reduction came from interventions made after an alert and before any failure, on components the alerts had identified.
questions.explanation: It traces the reduction to the specific mechanism claimed. D introduces a rival explanation for the same fall.

questions.prompt: An aquarium introduced a talk programme and reports that visitors who attend a talk stay longer and are more likely to donate. It plans to schedule talks continuously so that every visitor encounters one.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, casts most doubt on the plan?
options: A. Talks are given by volunteers.
B. Visitors who attend talks are those who arrived intending a long visit, and continuous talks would displace the quiet viewing that other visitors come for.
C. The talks last fifteen minutes.
D. Donation boxes are placed at the exit.
E. Some visitors attend more than one talk.
questions.explanation: It identifies both a selection effect and a cost the plan would impose on the visitors it does not currently serve.

questions.prompt: A driving test centre reports that candidates taking their test on a weekday morning pass more often than those testing on Saturday, and advises learners to book weekday slots.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the advice?
options: A. Saturday slots are more expensive.
B. Test routes are the same on all days.

C. Learners who can attend on a weekday morning are disproportionately those taking intensive courses with professional instructors, while Saturday candidates are mostly those fitting lessons around work.
D. Examiners work on a rota.
E. Some candidates travel from other towns.
questions.explanation: The pass difference tracks who can attend when, so booking a weekday slot does not transfer the advantage that produced the figure.

questions.prompt: A micro-brewery raised the price of its flagship beer and reports that revenue from that beer rose. The owner concludes that demand for it is insensitive to price.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. The brewery sells four other beers.
B. The price rise was announced in advance.
C. Production costs rose in the same period.
D. Sales volume of the flagship fell by a fifth, and much of that volume moved to the brewery's cheaper beers, whose margins are lower.
E. The beer is sold in bottles and casks.
questions.explanation: A fifth of volume lost is substantial sensitivity; revenue rose only because the remaining demand was inelastic enough, and the substitution cost the brewery margin elsewhere.

questions.prompt: A tourist board reports that visitors who use its official guided walks rate the city more highly than visitors who do not, and proposes funding more walks in order to improve the city's reputation.
questions.question: The proposal assumes which of the following?
options: A. The rating difference reflects the walks rather than the characteristics of visitors who choose to take one.
B. Guides can be recruited at current rates of pay.
C. Visitors rate cities consistently.
D. The walks are free to attend.
E. Ratings are collected at the end of a visit.
questions.explanation: Visitors who book a guided walk are already disposed to engage with the city, so the proposal needs the walk itself to be doing the work.

questions.prompt: Supporters of a proposal to convert a disused railway line into a footpath argue that it will bring visitors to the villages along the route. Opponents reply that walkers spend little money.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the opponents' reply?
options: A. Some walkers travel long distances to use such routes.
B. The conversion would be funded by a grant.
C. Walking is a popular activity.
D. The line passes through attractive countryside.

E. On comparable converted lines, the businesses that opened along the route - cafes, cycle hire, bed and breakfast - drew most of their trade from walkers, and village retail turnover rose measurably.
questions.explanation: Evidence from comparable conversions addresses the spending claim directly, and identifies the businesses through which the spending arrives.

questions.passageText:
Large firms with substantial research budgets routinely acquire small companies to obtain technologies they could, in principle, have developed themselves. The behaviour looks like an admission of failure and is better understood as a division of labour.

The asymmetry is in what each organisation is good at. A small company pursuing one idea can move quickly and, more importantly, can fail without consequence to anything else. A large firm allocating research funds must compare projects against each other and against established businesses, and a project threatening an existing product line faces internal opposition that has nothing to do with its merit. The result is that large firms are systematically better at improving what they already do and systematically worse at pursuing anything that would displace it.

Acquisition converts this weakness into a purchasing decision. The acquirer waits until uncertainty has been partly resolved, pays a price reflecting what is then known, and applies the assets a small company lacks: distribution, manufacturing, regulatory experience, capital.

The arrangement has known failure modes. Acquirers frequently destroy what they bought by imposing processes designed for a mature business on an operation whose value lay in not having them. Buying at the point of resolved uncertainty means paying for it, so the returns are unspectacular by design. And the possibility of acquisition shapes what small companies attempt: an inventor working toward a sale to a particular buyer builds what that buyer will want, which narrows the range of things attempted in ways nobody chose and no one is positioned to observe.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, a large firm is systematically worse at pursuing projects that
options: A. require substantial capital
B. involve regulatory approval
C. would displace an existing product line
D. originate outside its research department
E. take longer than a year to complete
questions.explanation: Internal opposition to such projects has nothing to do with their merit, which is the asymmetry the passage builds on.

questions.passageText:
Smallpox was eradicated in 1980. Polio, targeted since 1988 with more money and better technology, has not been, and the comparison is instructive about what makes a disease eliminable.

Smallpox had features that a campaign could exploit. Infection produced a visible rash, so cases could be found without laboratory confirmation; there was no animal reservoir; infected people were not contagious before symptoms appeared, so isolation worked; and one vaccination conferred durable protection, administered with a simple device by minimally trained staff. Together these permitted a strategy of finding each case and vaccinating around it, rather than vaccinating everyone.

Polio differs on nearly every point. Most infections produce no visible illness at all, so a single paralytic case implies many undetected ones and surveillance must test sewage rather than look at people. The oral vaccine requires multiple doses and a cold chain, and in rare cases the attenuated virus in it can regain the ability to circulate, so the campaign has had to manage outbreaks caused by its own principal tool.

The remaining obstacles are not primarily technical. Transmission persists where conflict prevents access, where vaccination teams have been attacked, and where a population has reason to distrust an externally funded campaign arriving in places that lack clean water and clinics. That last problem is not solved by better vaccines, and the general lesson is that the biological properties of a pathogen set what is possible while the conditions of delivery determine what is achieved.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, one feature that made smallpox eradicable was that
options: A. infected people were not contagious before symptoms appeared
B. it had an animal reservoir
C. most infections produced no visible illness
D. the vaccine required multiple doses
E. surveillance depended on testing sewage
questions.explanation: That property is what made isolation effective; the other options describe polio instead.

questions.passageTitle: Who Bears the Risk of Old Age
questions.passageText:
A pension promising a defined benefit — a proportion of final salary, for life — and one accumulating a defined contribution into a fund the retiree must convert into income are usually compared on generosity. The more consequential difference is who bears which risks.

Under a defined benefit, the sponsor bears investment risk, longevity risk and inflation risk, and the member bears the risk that the sponsor fails. Under a defined contribution, the member bears all three, and the sponsor's obligation ends when the contribution is paid. The shift from one to the other, which occurred across many countries within a generation, was therefore a transfer of risk to individuals, most of whom were not told this and could not have priced it if they had been.

The case for the shift was not baseless. Defined benefit promises proved more expensive than sponsors had assumed, because people lived longer and returns disappointed, and a promise that bankrupts its guarantor protects nobody. Defined benefit schemes also disadvantaged those who changed jobs frequently, which increasingly meant the young.

What has not been resolved is the problem the shift created. An individual approaching retirement with a fund faces decisions — how much to withdraw, how long to plan for, whether to buy an annuity at whatever rate prevails that year — that are genuinely difficult, cannot be practised, and have consequences that arrive too late to correct. Collective arrangements pooling longevity risk without a corporate guarantee are the obvious middle position, and their slow adoption reflects the difficulty of establishing new institutions rather than any argument that individual management is superior.
questions.prompt: Under a defined contribution arrangement, according to the passage, the member bears
options: A. only investment risk
B. investment, longevity and inflation risk
C. no risk once contributions are paid
D. only the risk that the sponsor fails
E. longevity risk alone
questions.explanation: The sponsor's obligation ends when the contribution is paid, which is the transfer the passage describes.

questions.passageText:
The question of how the Homeric poems were composed was transformed by fieldwork on an unrelated tradition. Researchers recording singers of long narrative songs in the Balkans in the 1930s found performers who could sustain metrical narrative for hours without a written text, and who produced a different version at each performance while insisting they sang it the same way every time.

The mechanism they described is formulaic. A singer commands a repertoire of phrases fitted to metrical positions, and larger units — arming, feasting, the arrival of a guest — that can be expanded or contracted as the occasion requires. Composition happens during performance rather than before it, and fluency comes from the system rather than from memorised text.

Applied to Homer, this explained features that had been treated as flaws: repeated epithets that seemed decorative, formulas apparently chosen for metre rather than sense, inconsistencies of detail across a long poem. These are the signature of oral composition rather than the residue of clumsy editing.

The theory has been refined rather than overturned. Its stronger versions claimed that formulaic composition excluded individual artistry, which the evidence does not support: singers within a tradition differ enormously in quality, and the surviving poems are not average specimens of anything. The defensible position is that the poems were made by a method that leaves recognisable traces, that the method was shared, and that what distinguishes these particular poems from the tradition producing them is a question the theory was never designed to answer and cannot settle.
questions.prompt: The Balkan singers described in the passage produced
options: A. a different version at each performance while insisting they sang it the same way
B. identical performances each time, as they claimed
C. written texts that were later memorised
D. songs of only a few minutes' duration
E. narratives composed entirely in advance
questions.explanation: The discrepancy between practice and self-description is part of what the fieldwork established.

Researchers recording singers of long narrative songs in the Balkans in the 1930s found performers who could sustain metrical narrative for hours without a written text, and who produced a different version at each performance while insisting they sang it the same way every time.

The mechanism they described is formulaic. A singer commands a repertoire of phrases fitted to metrical positions, and larger units — arming, feasting, the arrival of a guest — that can be expanded or contracted as the occasion requires. Composition happens during performance rather than before it, and fluency comes from the system rather than from memorised text.

Applied to Homer, this explained features that had been treated as flaws: repeated epithets that seemed decorative, formulas apparently chosen for metre rather than sense, inconsistencies of detail across a long poem. These are the signature of oral composition rather than the residue of clumsy editing.

The theory has been refined rather than overturned. Its stronger versions claimed that formulaic composition excluded individual artistry, which the evidence does not support: singers within a tradition differ enormously in quality, and the surviving poems are not average specimens of anything. The defensible position is that the poems were made by a method that leaves recognisable traces, that the method was shared, and that what distinguishes these particular poems from the tradition producing them is a question the theory was never designed to answer and cannot settle.
